Where does the outside operator walk on C‑201, and in what order?

From a plot plan to a walked route

  1. The plant in 3-Dwhat the model is built from, and what each block is

Interactive · the unit from the south-west

Every block comes from the plot plan

Click a number: positions, levels and lines are layout decisions, so the 3-D plant is only as true as the plot plan.

Interactive · station 1 in the tab

Six controls walk, show and record the round

Every arrival, reading and valve check writes a line to the event log, so the round is recorded as it is walked.

Interactive · plot plan, 60 × 44 m

Thirteen stations, west to east, up and back down

Walked
Climbed

The round crosses the plot once at grade, climbs C-201, then serves both structure decks before ending at the reflux pumps.

Interactive · floor height along the round

Most of the climbing is on one column

The map hides height. Unrolled along the path, the round is a ladder profile.

Floor
Climb so far

C-201 alone takes 22 of the 34.6 m climbed; stations 7–10 are where a round loses time and where fall protection matters.

Interactive · station cards

Recognise the station before you walk there

Each picture shows the items the 3-D station lists, so the trainee knows what to look for on arrival.

Interactive · identification exercise

Name every item without the tag plates

$$g=\frac{n_{ok}}{92}\times 100\ \%$$

$g$ grade, %; $n_{ok}$ items named right of the 92 on the round.

Grade
Target 90 %

The 90 % target needs 83 of 92 items: at most nine misses over thirteen stations. Equipment, valves and instruments all count.

Section summary

What part 1 settled

  • The 3-D plant is built from the plot plan and elevations; positions are layout decisions.
  • One round is 13 stations, 207 m long, with 34.6 m of climbing, mostly on C-201.
  • Arrivals, readings and valve checks are written to the event log.
  • Identification asks for 83 of the 92 items by name.

Part 2 · Reading points

What does the operator read on the round, and from which floor?

Part 2 · the plan

35 reading points on seven levels

  1. Levelsgrade, the drum tables, the column platforms and the structure decks

Interactive · elevation, looking north

Seven floors carry the 35 reading points

Twelve points are at grade; the other 23 need a ladder or a stair, and four floors are on C-201 alone.

Interactive · C-201 instruments

The tray fixes the nozzle; the platform fixes the climb

Levels say which floor. On the column, the tray decides the floor.

Nozzle EL
Read from floor

Column instruments sit at the tray they measure, so the round climbs to a platform within reach of each nozzle.

Interactive · station 10, EL +22.0

One close-up: tag, service, reading, line, height

A reading counts only when it is read in the field: the close-up writes Read PT-211 = 1.700 MPa g to the log.

Interactive · local indication

A local gauge shows the unit and decimals of the board

Shows at design
Where

The field value uses the board's unit and decimals, so a trainee can compare field and board directly.

Section summary

What part 2 settled

  • 35 reading points sit on seven floors; twelve are at grade.
  • Column thermowells are at their trays; four C-201 platforms carry twelve readings.
  • Only a field close-up writes a reading to the log.
  • Local values carry the board's units; a gauge glass reads in 5 % steps.

Part 3 · Valves and the rounds sheet

Is every hand valve where it should be, and what happens if it is not?

Part 3 · the plan

Line-up first, then write it down

  1. Normal positions21 valves in the scene: open, closed, car-sealed, throttled
  2. Closed blockswhat a shut suction, discharge, bypass or drain does in the model
  3. Field valvessteps of 0, 25, 50, 100 % and how they scale a utility
  4. The rounds sheet and the log28 rows checked against the plant, and the trail a round leaves

Interactive · hand valves in the scene

Each valve has a normal position

Sixteen valves are open or shut, four throttle a utility, one is drawn for orientation only; car-sealed valves refuse without a permit.

Interactive · station 3, the feed control station

Colour and close-up tell the position

Normal and now are printed side by side, so an off-normal valve is seen in the field, not inferred from the board.

Interactive · feed pumps P-201A/B, station 2

A running pump needs both blocks open

The table says what to expect; a shut block shows why it matters.

Running:

The spare's blocks stay open so it can start on demand; a shut block on the running pump starves or dead-heads it.

Interactive · FV-201 station and the drains

Blocks, bypass and drains each move a flow

An open bypass carries about 54 m³/h alone and an open drain loses 6–8 m³/h; only the field shows their position.

Interactive · rounds sheet, 28 rows

Each answer is checked within a gauge tolerance

Simulated time
Lines

Section summary

What part 3 settled

  • 21 valves in the scene: 16 open or shut, 4 throttling, 1 for orientation only.
  • Car-sealed PSV-201 blocks refuse to move without a permit.
  • A shut block starves, dead-heads, diverts or drains; the model shows each effect.
  • 28 sheet rows are checked against the live plant, within gauge tolerance.

This deck

Key Takeaways

1

Walk the same 13 stations in the same order every round.

2

Climb to each platform; read the gauge, never guess it from the board.

3

Compare every hand valve with its normal position, and report any difference.

4

Leave car-sealed valves alone unless a permit says otherwise.

5

Write each reading on the rounds sheet at the station, not afterwards.
